ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in the figure, a rough inclined plane with an angle $\theta=37^{\circ}$ is sufficiently long. On the inclined plane, there is a wooden board with mass $M=1\mathrm{kg}$. At time $t=0$, another wooden block with mass $m=1\mathrm{kg}$ (which can be considered as a point mass) moves up the board with an initial velocity $v_{0}=20\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$ from the lower end of the board. Simultaneously, a force $F=14\mathrm{N}$ is applied to the board along the inclined plane, causing the board to start moving from rest. At $t=2\mathrm{s}$, the force $F$ is removed. It is known that the coefficient of kinetic friction between the board and the block is $\mu_{1}=0.25$, and the coefficient of kinetic friction between the board and the inclined plane is $\mu_{2}=0.5$. The maximum static friction is equal to the kinetic friction. Find: ($\sin37^{\circ}=$ 0.6, $\cos37^{\circ}=0.8$, $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$)

1. What are the accelerations of the block and the plank within the first 2 seconds?
2. To prevent the block from sliding off the upper end of the board, how long should the board be at least?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
The acceleration of the block $a_{1}=8\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$ is directed downward along the incline; the acceleration of the plank $a_{2}=2\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$ is directed upward along the incline.
$20.3\mathrm{m}$

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, the inclined plane is lower on the right and higher on the left, and the right end is marked with angle θ; the plank is placed on the inclined plane, and the small block is located at the lower end near the right side of the plank. The v0 arrow beside the small block points along the plank surface toward the upper left, indicating that the initial velocity of the block is upward along the inclined plane; the F arrow on the left side of the plank also points along the inclined plane toward the upper left, indicating that the external force pulls the plank upward along the inclined plane. Then reason: Take upward along the inclined plane as positive. The block initially slides upward relative to the plank, so the friction force exerted by the plank on the block is downward along the inclined plane, with magnitude f1=mu1*m*g*cos37=0.25*1*10*0.8=2 N; the friction force exerted by the block on the plank is upward along the inclined plane. The normal pressure between the plank and the inclined plane is (M+m)gcos37, so f2=mu2*(M+m)*g*cos37=0.5*2*10*0.8=8 N. During the first 2 s, the plank moves upward, and the friction force exerted by the inclined plane on the plank is downward along the inclined plane. 0<t<2 s: For the block, a1=-(mg sin37+f1)/m=-(1*10*0.6+2)/1=-8 m/s^2, that is, the magnitude is 8 m/s^2, and the direction is downward along the inclined plane. For the plank, a2=(F+f1-Mg sin37-f2)/M=(14+2-1*10*0.6-8)/1=2 m/s^2, that is, the direction is upward along the inclined plane. At t=2 s, the displacement of the block is x1=v0*t+0.5*a1*t^2=20*2+0.5*(-8)*4=24 m, and the velocity is v1=20-8*2=4 m/s; the displacement of the plank is x2=0.5*a2*t^2=0.5*2*4=4 m, and the velocity is v2=2*2=4 m/s. Therefore, the block has already moved upward relative to the plank by 24-4=20 m. After F is removed, the plank still moves upward for a period of time. At this time, the block still has a tendency to slide upward relative to the plank, and the friction direction remains unchanged. The acceleration of the block is still -8 m/s^2; the acceleration of the plank is a2'=(f1-Mg sin37-f2)/M=(2-6-8)/1=-12 m/s^2. The time required for the plank to decelerate from 4 m/s to 0 is Δt=4/12=1/3 s. During this interval, the displacement of the block is 4*(1/3)+0.5*(-8)*(1/3)^2=8/9 m, and the displacement of the plank is 4*(1/3)+0.5*(-12)*(1/3)^2=2/3 m, so the relative displacement increases by 8/9-2/3=2/9 m. When the plank stops, the velocity of the block is 4-8*(1/3)=4/3 m/s. At this time, if the plank remains stationary, the plank is subjected to its own gravity along the inclined plane downward of 6 N and the friction force exerted by the block on the plank upward along the inclined plane of 2 N, so a static friction force of 4 N upward from the inclined plane to the plank is needed; the maximum static friction force is 8 N, so the plank can be kept stationary. Thus the block continues to slide upward on the stationary plank, the magnitude of the deceleration is still 8 m/s^2, and the additional sliding distance is (4/3)^2/(2*8)=1/9 m. The maximum relative displacement is 20+2/9+1/9=61/3 m≈20.3 m, so the shortest length of the plank should be about 20.3 m.
